# All texts of the app. Placeholders such as {y} are filled per table; the full list is in # apps-src/regtab-dev/PLAN.md (sections "Explanations" and "Questions"). Strings written r"(...)" are raw: # backslashes in them are typed once, as in LaTeX, e.g. r"(\(\alpha = 0.05\))". # ---- Links used in the texts below ---- lk <- local({ a <- function(u, i, t) sprintf('%s %s', u, i, t) yt <- paste0('', fontawesome::fa("youtube"), "") list(tab = a("https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_oDiAMQj1hM&t=43", yt, "GLM Regression Table"), od = a("https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJm6eN5ZDzk", yt, "Overdispersion")) }) # ---- Top of the page (Explore and Quiz) ---- pg <- list( intro = "Each new table simulates a data set from the model you choose, fits that model in R, and prints its summary() exactly as R shows it. In Quiz mode, each table comes with a question about the output. In Explore mode, hover over (or tap) any part of the output to see what it means; the equation below the table and the plot of the resulting model show the coefficient you select. Switch to Explore at any time to study the same table. The app assumes a significance level of \\(\\alpha = 0.05\\).", # ---- Below the introduction, in a version for one chapter (?v= in the app's address) ---- ver = list( lm = "This version of the app is for the chapter Ordinary Linear Models: linear models with at most one continuous explanatory variable.", glm = "This version of the app is for the chapter Generalized Linear Models: models with at most one continuous explanatory variable.", dummy = "This version of the app is for the chapter Dummy Variables: models with categorical explanatory variables, without interaction."), # ---- Explore: the button "What am I looking at?" ---- # TODO(author): drafted text; adjust or approve wh = list( t = "What am I looking at?", b = r"(
  • The table is the summary() of a model fitted in R, to a data set simulated from the model you chose under Family and Explanatory variables. New table simulates a new data set.
  • Hover over (or tap) any part of the output to see what it means, in the box next to the plot.
  • Below the table is the equation of the fitted model. When you select a coefficient, the equation and the plot show it too.
  • The plot shows the data as points, and the fitted model. For a GLM, it shows the model on the scale of the outcome and on the scale of the model (\(\eta\)).
  • The section Explanation at the bottom of the page describes the models and the statistical terms.
)"), # ---- Bottom of the page (Explore): one collapsible section per entry, named by its title ---- expl = list( "Models" = paste( "
", r"(
Normal
An ordinary linear model, fitted with lm(): \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1 + \dots + \epsilon\), with normally distributed \(\epsilon\).
)", r"(
Poisson
A GLM for counts with a log link, fitted with glm(..., family = poisson): \(\log(\lambda) = \eta\).
)", r"(
Binomial (binary)
A GLM for outcomes that are 0 or 1, with a logit link, fitted with glm(..., family = binomial): \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \eta\).
)", "
Binomial
The same GLM for a number of successes out of a number of trials, fitted with glm(cbind(successes, trials - successes) ~ ..., family = binomial).
", r"(
Continuous
Can take on any value within a range, like \(1, 1.001, 1.01, \dots\).
)", "
Categorical
Can only take on specific values, like red, green, blue. The first category in alphabetical order is taken to be the reference group. Second (categorical) adds a second explanatory variable (for ease of visualization, this is always a categorical variable).
", "
Interaction
When you enable interaction, the effect of one variable can differ depending on the value of the other (i.e., different slopes for continuous, and difference-in-differences for two-way categorical).
", "
"), # Three groups; the lm version hides the GLM group and the group headings "Statistical terminology" = paste( "
All models
", "
", "
\\(y\\) — response variable
The outcome.
", "
\\(x\\) — explanatory variable
The variable the outcome is regressed on.
", "
", "
Ordinary linear models
", "
", r"(
\(\epsilon\) — error
Difference between the true population values of the outcome and those predicted by the true model. \(\epsilon\) is the true error. \(\hat{\epsilon}\) is sometimes used to denote the residual, an 'estimate' of the error.
)", r"(
\(\beta_0\) — intercept
Mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero. \(\hat{\beta}_0\) (beta-hat) is its estimate.
)", r"(
\(\beta_1\) — slope
Change in the mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by 1. \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (beta-hat) is its estimate.
)", "
", "
", "
Generalized linear models
", "
", r"(
\(\eta\) — linear predictor
The function that describes the relationship between the explanatory variable and the (transformed) mean of the outcome.
)", r"(
\(\beta_0\) — intercept
Mean of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero. \(\hat{\beta}_0\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a Poisson GLM with log-link, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the mean count at \(x=0\). For a binomial GLM with logit-link, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the mean odds at \(x=0\).
)", paste0(r"(
\(\beta_1\) — slope
Change in the mean of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by 1. \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a Poisson GLM with log-link, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in mean count when \(x\) increases by 1 (see: )", lk$tab, r"(). For a binomial GLM with logit-link, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in mean odds when \(x\) increases by 1. No direct interpretation in terms of probability is possible.
)"), # TODO(author): name the inverse link function (exp for Poisson, exp / (1 + exp) for binomial), used by qs$mis$link r"(
Link function
A function that stretches the possible range of the mean of the distribution from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). This ensures the model can only predict valid values. For a Poisson GLM, that means non-negative counts (the natural logarithm: \(\log(\lambda)\)). For a binomial GLM, that means probabilities between \(0\) and \(1\) (the logarithm of the odds, or logit: \(\log \left( \frac{p}{1-p} \right)\)).
)", paste0(r"(
Dispersion
In most GLMs, the mean and variance are related: for a Poisson distribution the variance equals the mean, and for a binomial distribution with \(n\) trials it is \(n p (1 - p)\). Dispersion compares the variance of the outcome with this assumed mean-variance relationship. Overdispersion means more variance than the model predicts, underdispersion less. See: )", lk$od, ".
